Modal confirmation on the native `<dialog>`, with `role="alertdialog"`. It interrupts to ask
one question, so it has no close button and no light dismiss: only the two actions, or
Escape (which counts as cancel), close it. Initial focus lands on the cancel action, so a

the grid, arrows move by day and week, Home and End jump to the ends of the week, Page Up
and Page Down change month, Shift with them changes year, Enter or Space selects.

declarations.description:
Text field with a suggestions list, after the ARIA 1.2 combobox pattern. The app feeds the
suggestions: on each keystroke the field fires `ht-input` and the app replaces the
`ht-combobox-option` children (optionally inside `ht-combobox-group`). The combobox never
filters, sorts or fetches.

The list is a listbox in a manual popover in the top layer, under the field and as wide as it.
It flips above the field when there is no room below. It opens on typing, on Up or Down, and
on a click in the field, and only when it has something to show: options, the loading row, the
empty row, or the create row. Focus stays in the text box; the highlighted option is linked
with `aria-activedescendant`.

Keys: Up and Down move through the options and the create row, and wrap. Nothing is
highlighted until you press one, so Enter on its own submits the text (`ht-submit`); with an
option highlighted, Enter picks it (`ht-select`). Escape closes the list and keeps the text; a
second Escape clears it. Alt+Down opens the list without moving, Alt+Up closes it. Home and End
stay in the text box. Hovering an option only highlights it visually, so a resting pointer
never changes what Enter does.

Picking an option fills the field with the option's text, unless the `ht-select` handler set
`value` itself (for example to clear the field after linking a ticket).

Prefix and suffix content (a scope picker, a project) sits inside the field as inset chips.
The combobox does not disable slotted controls: disable them yourself along with the field.

Screen readers: a polite status region reads "Searching…", the empty text, or the result
count while the list is open. Where the browser cannot link the text box to a slotted option
by reference (`ariaActiveDescendantElement`), the highlighted option is read there instead.

declarations.description:
One day on a vertical hour axis: meetings and planned tasks placed by start and end time, with the
hours in a left gutter. Items that overlap share the width in equal columns. A now line marks the
current time. Items with no `start` go to a folding Anytime group under the axis.

Put `ht-schedule-item` children in it, in any order. It places them; it does not fetch, edit or
move them. Other children are not shown.

For screen readers the axis is a list of the items in time order, whatever their order in the
DOM, and each item says its time first ("10:00 to 11:00, Design sync"). Name the list with `label`
or a host `aria-label`.

**Now line.** Set `now` to fix it (`11:42`). Without `now`, when `date` is today, it follows the
clock: it moves once a minute and pauses while the page is hidden. Without either, there is no
line.

**Drop target.** With `droppable`, the axis takes items dragged from an `ht-sortable-list` whose
`group` is in `accept` (any group when `accept` is empty). It answers the list's `ht-drag-over`,
snaps the pointer to 15 minutes and draws a dashed 30-minute box with the time range. On the drop
the source list fires `ht-reorder` with `to` set to this schedule and
`data: { time: '13:15', date: '2026-10-26' }`. Save the time and re-render; the schedule never moves
DOM itself. Only the axis takes drops, not the Anytime group.

declarations.description:
File picker with a drop zone. A real `<input type="file">` drives it, so Tab, Enter and Space
and screen readers get the native control; the zone around it is its label, and dropping files
on it works too. Chosen files show in a list under the zone, each with a remove button.

Form-associated: submits one entry per file under `name`, so the form needs
`enctype="multipart/form-data"`. `required` blocks submit until a file is chosen, and form reset
clears the list. Files can only come from the person: the browser does not restore them.

Checks run in the order type (`accept`), size (`max-size`), count (`max-files`, or one without
`multiple`). A turned-away file never enters `files`: it fires `ht-reject`, the reason shows under
the zone, and a polite live region reads it out, as it does for added and removed files.

and each listed file draws a thin bar with a `progressbar` role. Delete the entry to drop the bar.

declarations.description:
A live clock that counts up from `start`: time spent on a task, a call, a running job. It shows
`h:mm:ss`, or with `compact` `mm:ss` under an hour and `h:mm` from an hour on.

Running, it is an accent chip with a pulsing dot. `paused` turns it into a neutral chip with a
pause glyph and freezes the time at `paused-at` (or at the moment `paused` was set). `bare` drops
the chip and leaves plain tabular digits in the mono face that take their size and colour from
the host, for tight spots.

The clock always counts from `start`. Resuming does not subtract the paused span: when a paused
clock runs again, the app moves `start` forward by the time it spent paused.

It ticks with one timer aligned to the next whole second of elapsed time (the next whole minute
for `compact` above an hour). While the page is hidden it stops; when the page shows it recomputes
from `start`, so it never drifts. A `start` in the future shows zero until it arrives. Without a
readable `start` it renders nothing and takes no space.

It is a `timer` whose accessible name holds whole minutes only ("1 hour 24 minutes elapsed",
with ", paused" when paused), so it changes once a minute and nothing is read every second. The
visible digits sit in a `<time>` with a machine-readable duration (`datetime="PT1H24M7S"`).

declarations.description:
A bar split into parts side by side, each with a value and a tone: "3 meetings, 2 done,
4 open, 1 late". Parts are `ht-meter-part` children.

Without `max`, the parts share the full width. With `max`, each part takes `value / max` and the
room left is a hatched track. When the parts add up to more than `max`, the bar scales to the
sum and a 2px mark shows where `max` falls.

The bar is `role="img"`, named by a summary generated from the parts ("10 of 12: 3 meetings,
2 done, 4 open, 1 late", "14 of 12, over by 2: 4 meetings, 10 open"), with `label` (or a host
`aria-label`, which is forwarded) in front. Labels are lower-cased as they are, with no
plurals worked out: set `summary` when the generated text does not read well.

`legend` adds a table of parts with their counts. Parts at 0 keep their row there, so a set of
meters shows the same rows. While the summary is generated, the legend is hidden from screen
readers, because the bar already reads every part. When `summary` is set, the legend is exposed
as a list, since the custom text may leave the counts out.

declarations.description:
Page control for lists and tables: Previous, the page numbers, Next. Long ranges keep the first
and last page and fold the rest into ellipses, with a constant number of slots so the buttons do
not move under the pointer as the page changes.

The page count is `total-pages` when set, else `total` divided by `page-size`, rounded up, else 1.
With `total` and `page-size` both set, a range summary ("21–40 of 312") sits before the controls.
A `page` outside the range is drawn as the nearest end but never rewritten, so it survives a
`total` that arrives later. The control stays visible with one page; hide it yourself if you
prefer.

Without `href` the pages are buttons and the element keeps `page` itself. With `href` they are
links built from the template, for server-rendered lists. Either way a click fires
`ht-page-change` first; cancel it to keep the page (and, for links, to stop the navigation) and
route yourself. Modified clicks on links (Cmd, Ctrl, Shift, Alt, middle button) are left to the
browser.

Renders a `<nav>` landmark. Name it with `label`, or `aria-label` on the element (forwarded to
the nav). Page changes are announced politely as "Page 3 of 16".
declarations.name: HtPagination

Non-modal panel anchored to a trigger. The panel is a manual popover in the top layer, so
it is never clipped, and it is positioned in JavaScript: it flips to the opposite side when
there is no room and is clamped to the viewport.

The first element in the default slot is the trigger. It gets `aria-haspopup="dialog"`,
`aria-expanded`, and `aria-controls` pointing at the first element in the `content` slot
(the panel itself lives in the shadow root, which an id reference cannot cross). Focus moves
into the panel on open and returns to the trigger on Escape or when `hide()` runs while focus
is inside. Focus is not trapped. Escape, a press outside, or tabbing out closes it.

The trigger must be focusable and activate on click (a button or `ht-button`).

centre along the panel edge and swaps sides when the panel flips.

listbox in the top layer, so it is never clipped and it stays above an open `ht-dialog`.
It flips above the trigger when there is no room below, and scroll arrows appear when the list

Put `ht-option` children in it (optionally inside `ht-option-group`, with `ht-separator` or
`<hr>` between). An `ht-option` can hold any content: icons, two lines, badges. Set its `label`
when the content is more than a name, so the trigger and typeahead have a short text.

with `ht-option` in one select.

picks a matching option without opening. In the list, arrows move, Home and End jump, PageUp and
PageDown move by ten, Enter or Space picks, Escape closes, and typing jumps to a match. Pressing
the trigger with a mouse and releasing over an option picks it. The trade: there is no native

declarations.description:
A list the user reorders by dragging, and the source of every drag in Halftone. Items are
`ht-sortable-item` children. A grip at the start of each row starts the drag; the row keeps its
own buttons and clicks. A 2px accent line with a ring dot marks the landing spot, and a lifted,
slightly tilted copy of the item follows the pointer while the original stays in place at 35%.

**It never moves DOM.** On drop it fires `ht-reorder`; the app saves the new order and renders
it. Same rule as `ht-table`, which fires `sort` and never sorts.

Pointer: the drag starts after 5px of movement on the grip. Touch: press and hold the grip for
250ms (moving first scrolls the page instead). Near the top or bottom edge of the nearest
scrolling area the area scrolls, faster closer to the edge. Esc cancels.

Keyboard, on the grip: Space or Enter picks the item up, Up and Down (and Home, End) move the
landing line, Space or Enter drops, Esc or Tab cancels. Each step is announced in a polite live
region. Keyboard moves stay inside the list; a move to another list or day belongs in the app's
Move To menu.

`handle="none"` drops the grip and lets the whole row drag. A press on a control inside the row
(button, link, field, checkbox) does not start a drag. On touch the row keeps page scrolling: a
hold of 250ms without moving picks the item up. Keyboard users still get a grip button: it is
visually hidden and draws a focus ring around the row when focused.

**Drag protocol.** Drops cross components through DOM events, so no file imports another. While
a pointer drag runs, the list fires these on other elements (all `CustomEvent`, `composed`, with
an `HtDragDetail`):

- `ht-drag-over` on the deepest element under the pointer: bubbles, cancelable. A target that
  takes the item calls `preventDefault()` and fills `detail.target` (defaults to the element it
  was fired on), and may fill `detail.data` and `detail.label`. A handler that sees
  `defaultPrevented` already set does nothing, so the deepest target wins. Fired once per
  animation frame while the pointer moves or the page scrolls.
- `ht-drag-leave` on the previous target, directly (no bubbling): the pointer left it, or the
  drag ended without a drop on it (Esc, a drop on nothing, the pointer cancelled, the item
  removed). Fired before the next target hears `ht-drag-over`.
- `ht-drag-drop` on the accepting target, directly: the item was dropped on it. Same detail as
  the last `ht-drag-over`.

A list takes items from itself and from lists with the same non-empty `group`, and sets
`detail.data` to `{ index }`. Lists without a `group` keep their items to themselves.
declarations.name: HtSortableList

Numbered steps for a wizard header or a setup guide: an ordered list of `ht-step` children,
each with a marker (01, 02…) joined to the next by a connector. Markers turn into a tick
when the step is done, and connectors after done steps take the accent.

Set `current` to the index or `value` of the current step. Steps before it are done and
steps after it upcoming, unless a step sets its own `state`. Without `current` the steps
are a plain numbered list, which suits a setup guide.

`orientation="vertical"` stacks the steps and shows each step's slotted content under its
heading, indented past the marker, with the connector running down the side.

Horizontal steps that do not fit their width collapse: only the current step keeps its
visible label (the others stay readable to screen readers), and if the markers still do
not fit the row scrolls sideways. It never widens the page.

Steps are not interactive by default: a wizard's own Back and Next buttons drive
`current`. With `clickable`, done steps become buttons; add `nonlinear` to make upcoming
steps buttons too. The buttons sit in the normal tab order (no roving focus): a step list
is a list of links back, not a composite widget, and it rarely has more than a handful.

Data table made of custom elements. Layout uses `display: table*` on the hosts, and each
host carries its own ARIA role (`table`, `rowgroup`, `row`, `columnheader`, `cell`), so
assistive technology sees an ordinary table. Give it an accessible name with `aria-label`.

```html
<ht-table aria-label="Projects">
  <ht-table-head><ht-table-row>
    <ht-table-header sortable key="name">Name</ht-table-header>
    <ht-table-header align="end">Events</ht-table-header>
  </ht-table-row></ht-table-head>
  <ht-table-body>
    <ht-table-row><ht-table-cell>sentinel</ht-table-cell><ht-table-cell align="end">1,204</ht-table-cell></ht-table-row>
  </ht-table-body>
</ht-table>
```

response. Only one header shows a sort direction at a time.

The table scrolls horizontally when it is wider than its container, and joins the
tab order while it does, so keyboard users can scroll it. For a sticky header, set
`sticky-header` and give the table a height with `--ht-table-max-height`.

A week as a row of day tabs. Each tab is a column whose background rises with the day's load,
with a split bar at its foot (an `ht-meter size="sm"` in the tab's `meter` slot). Today's date is
underlined in accent; the selected day is accent-soft.

It is a tab list. Arrow keys move and select (Home and End jump to the ends), with one tab stop
that follows the selection. Disabled days are skipped. When `value` matches no tab, nothing is
selected and the tab stop falls on today, else the first enabled day; `value` is left alone.

Each `ht-week-tab` with `droppable` takes items dragged from an `ht-sortable-list` (see the
drag protocol): it draws a 2px accent inset ring while an item is over it, and the source list
fires `ht-reorder` with `data: { date }` on drop. The strip never moves anything itself.
declarations.name: HtWeekStrip

declarations.description:
One day inside `ht-week-strip`. Shows the weekday and the date, a fill that rises with `load`,
and whatever sits in the `meter` slot at its foot.

Its accessible name is built from its attributes: "Mon 26, today", plus `summary` when set
("Mon 26, today, 2 meetings, 3 done"). Set `summary` to the same text as the slotted meter's
summary, since the tab's name replaces its content. An `aria-label` you set yourself wins.

With `droppable` it is a drop target in the drag protocol. It takes an item when the source
list's `group` is in `accept` (or `accept` is empty), and is not `disabled`. It fills
`detail.data` with `{ date: value }` and `detail.label` with "Mon 26". A target nested inside
the tab that takes the item first wins.
declarations.name: HtWeekTab
